title: The (Few) Things I Track
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. describes the small, deliberately analog set of trackers that keeps his classroom practice simple and sustainable. He frames the problem as two opposite failure modes: tracking so much that the system collapses as data piles up, or tracking so little that the teacher's memory carries too much of the load. His answer is a short list of trackers tied to the practices he considers high-leverage: mini-sermon attempts (aiming for at least 100 a year to strengthen students' belief that school has value), classroom-management 'builds' logged on index cards, 2x10 relationship interventions, attempted moments of genuine connection with the often-neglected middle group of students, and Pop-Up Debate participation as formative data. The move of the piece is to connect tracking to his broader motivation framework, treating what a teacher chooses to count as a way of making sure the most important but easily neglected habits actually happen. It ends by inviting colleagues to reflect on what they themselves keep track of.
points: Stuart names two opposite tracking failures: tracking too much to sustain over a year, and tracking too little so that memory has to carry what a simple external record could hold.
He tracks mini-sermons because every teacher gives them but rarely often enough, and frequent attempts by credible teachers are a largely unused lever for students' belief that school is valuable.
The 2x10 intervention depends on ten consecutive non-academic conversations with one student, so he keeps a separate ten-checkbox record and runs only two or three per year.
A clipboard for attempted moments of genuine connection is aimed at the oft-neglected middle group of students rather than the most visible ones.
His Pop-Up Debate tracker began after a principal marked him down for not tracking formative data, showing how a minimal tool can satisfy evaluation demands while staying useful.
quotes: I track too many things, and as a result, I can't maintain the tracking system as the year progresses and the data piles up.
I track too few things, and as a result, I place too much burden on my mind to remember stuff that could be better remembered through externalizing my memory onto a tracking device.

The trouble is NOT that we never do these; it's that we don't do them nearly enough. Mini-sermons — especially when given by Credible teachers — are, therefore, a largely disused lever for improving the Value belief in our schools.

Because the effectiveness of this intervention depends on having 10 consecutive non-academic conversations with the target student, I keep track of these in a separate spot from my MGC clipboard. I simply jot down the target student's initials and create 10 checkboxes.

This clipboard sheet has one job: tracking my attempted moments of genuine connection. As I wrote about earlier this week, the power of this list comes from the oft-neglected middle group of students.

I started keeping a separate clipboard sheet for these when my principal lovingly dinged me on an eval for not tracking formative data in a distinguished manner. The tracker is nonetheless very simple and allows me to keep notes on how individual students are developing.
